```{r setup}
library(nbzinbHossen)
library(MASS)
library(pscl)
data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")
data("NMES1988", package = "AER")
kable <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, booktabs = TRUE, ...)
```

# Introduction

Many data in health research are counts: the number of hospital visits in a
month, or the number of research papers published. Poisson regression is
useful in that case, but it has a very strong assumption: the mean and the
variance must be equal. This is rarely true in a real data set. Most count
data are overdispersed, with a variance greater than the mean, and many data
sets also contain more zeros than a Poisson distribution allows.

The negative binomial (NB2) model handles overdispersion with a dispersion
parameter $\theta$, so that $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$. When the
extra zeros come from a different process, for example a person who never
sees a doctor, a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model fits more
naturally. It treats each observation either as a structural zero or as a
draw from an NB distribution, which can itself be zero.

In this project, I built the R package **nbzinbHossen**, which fits both
models:

- NB regression by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), alternated
  with Newton–Raphson updates of $\log\theta$;
- ZINB regression by an EM algorithm whose M-steps are IRLS fits.

I did not use any general-purpose optimizer such as `optim()`, or `glm()`
fitting code. I check the package against `MASS::glm.nb()` and
`pscl::zeroinfl()` on two data sets, test by simulation whether `zinbreg()`
recovers known parameters, and use it to analyse the NMES1988 data.

# Methods

## Negative binomial (NB2) regression

For counts $Y_i$ with covariates $x_i$, offset $o_i$ and prior weights $a_i$,
$$
P(Y_i = y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!}
\Big(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big)^{\theta}
\Big(\frac{\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big)^{y},
\qquad \log\mu_i = \eta_i = x_i^\top\beta + o_i,
$$
so $E(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i+\mu_i^2/\theta$. The
log-likelihood is
$$
\ell(\beta,\theta)=\sum_i a_i\big[\log\Gamma(y_i+\theta)-\log\Gamma(\theta)
-\log y_i!+\theta\log\theta+y_i\log\mu_i-(\theta+y_i)\log(\theta+\mu_i)\big].
$$

**IRLS for $\beta$ ($\theta$ fixed).** With the log link,
$(\partial\mu/\partial\eta)^2=\mu^2$, so Fisher scoring is weighted least
squares with
$$
w_i = a_i\frac{\theta\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i},\qquad
z_i = (\eta_i-o_i) + \frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\mu_i},\qquad
\beta^{(t+1)} = (X^\top W X)^{-1}X^\top W z .
$$
The solve uses the QR decomposition of $W^{1/2}X$. Because the log link is
not canonical for the NB, a Fisher-scoring step is not guaranteed to
increase $\ell$, so the step is halved whenever $\ell$ would decrease.

**Newton–Raphson for $\theta$ ($\beta$ fixed).** With $\psi$ and $\psi'$ the
digamma and trigamma functions,
$$
U(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi(y_i+\theta)-\psi(\theta)+\log\theta+1-\log(\theta+\mu_i)-\frac{y_i+\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big],
$$
$$
H(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi'(y_i+\theta)-\psi'(\theta)+\frac1\theta-\frac{2}{\theta+\mu_i}+\frac{y_i+\theta}{(\theta+\mu_i)^2}\Big].
$$
We update $\phi=\log\theta$, which keeps $\theta>0$:
$U_\phi=\theta U$, $H_\phi=\theta^2H+\theta U$, $\phi\leftarrow\phi-U_\phi/H_\phi$.
If $H_\phi\ge 0$ a unit step in the direction of $U_\phi$ is taken, and
steps are halved until $\ell$ does not decrease.

**Outer loop.** Start from a Poisson IRLS fit and the moment estimate
$\theta_0=\sum_i a_i/\sum_i a_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)^2$. Then alternate the two
updates until $|\ell^{(t+1)}-\ell^{(t)}|<10^{-8}$. If $\theta$ reaches a
large cap ($10^6$) the data show no overdispersion and a warning is given.

**Standard errors.** As in `glm.nb()`,
$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat WX)^{-1}$ treating $\theta$ as
known, and $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\{-H(\hat\theta)\}^{-1/2}$.

## Zero-inflated negative binomial regression

With probability $\pi_i$ observation $i$ is a structural zero, otherwise it
is NB$(\mu_i,\theta)$:
$$
P(Y_i=0)=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0(\mu_i,\theta),\quad
P(Y_i=y)=(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(y;\mu_i,\theta),\ y\ge1,
$$
where $f_0=\{\theta/(\theta+\mu_i)\}^\theta$, $\log\mu_i=x_i^\top\beta+o_i$
and $\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i=z_i^\top\gamma$. The observed-data
log-likelihood
$$
\ell(\beta,\gamma,\theta)=\sum_{y_i=0}\log\big[\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0\big]
+\sum_{y_i>0}\big[\log(1-\pi_i)+\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)\big]
$$
contains the log of a sum, so it is not an exponential-family GLM
likelihood and cannot be maximized by IRLS directly. We use the EM
algorithm with latent indicators $D_i=1$ for structural zeros.

**E-step.**
$\tau_i=P(D_i=1\mid y_i)=\pi_i/\{\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0\}$ if $y_i=0$, and
$\tau_i=0$ if $y_i>0$.

**M-step, zero part.** Maximize
$\sum_i[\tau_i\log\pi_i+(1-\tau_i)\log(1-\pi_i)]$: a logistic regression
with fractional response $\tau_i$, fitted by IRLS with
$w_i=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ and $z_i=z_i^\top\gamma+(\tau_i-\pi_i)/\{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\}$.

**M-step, count part.** Maximize
$\sum_i(1-\tau_i)\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)$: exactly the NB fit above
with prior weights $a_i=1-\tau_i$, warm-started at the current
$(\beta,\theta)$.

**Starting values and convergence.** $(\beta,\theta)$ come from the NB fit
and $\gamma$ from an IRLS logistic regression of $I(y_i=0)$ on $z_i$. EM
stops when $\ell$ changes by less than $10^{-10}$. The package records
$\ell$ at every iteration and warns if it ever decreases. This never
happened in any fit reported here.

**Standard errors (analytic Hessian).** EM gives no standard errors, so we
invert the observed information of $\ell$ in $(\beta,\gamma,\log\theta)$.
Each $\ell_i$ depends on $\beta$ only through $\eta_i$ and on $\gamma$ only
through $\zeta_i=z_i^\top\gamma$. The Hessian is therefore built from
per-observation second derivatives, e.g.
$H_{\beta\beta}=X^\top\mathrm{diag}(a_i\,\partial^2\ell_i/\partial\eta_i^2)X$.
For $y_i>0$ these are NB and logistic derivatives, e.g.
$\partial^2\ell_i/\partial\eta_i^2=-\theta\mu_i(\theta+y_i)/(\theta+\mu_i)^2$.
For $y_i=0$, write $\ell_i=\log L_i$ with
$L_i=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i}$ and $g_i=\theta\log\{\theta/(\theta+\mu_i)\}$.
With $r_i=(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i}/L_i=1-\tau_i$ and $\partial r_i/\partial g_i=r_i(1-r_i)$,
$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial u\,\partial v}=r_i\,g_{i,uv}+r_i(1-r_i)\,g_{i,u}\,g_{i,v},
\qquad u,v\in\{\eta_i,\log\theta\},
$$
and the cross terms with $\zeta_i$ are
$-\pi_i(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i}g_{i,u}/L_i^2$. All terms are listed in
`R/zinb_hessian.R`. The analytic Hessian agrees with
`numDeriv::hessian()` to about $10^{-7}$ relative error (checked in the
tests). We report $\log\theta$ with its SE, as `zeroinfl()` does, and
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\hat\theta\,\mathrm{SE}(\log\hat\theta)$ by the
delta method.

# The R package

The package **nbzinbHossen** is installed with

```r
devtools::install_github("armanhossen-am/nbzinbHossen")
```

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `nbreg(formula, data, subset, na.action, weights, offset, control)` | NB regression by IRLS + Newton–Raphson for $\log\theta$ |
| `zinbreg(formula, data, subset, na.action, weights, offset, control)` | ZINB regression by EM with IRLS M-steps; formula `y ~ count | zero` |
| `nbreg_control()`, `zinbreg_control()` | tolerances, iteration limits, `trace`, Hessian type |

Both functions return S3 objects (`"nbreg"`, `"zinbreg"`) holding the
coefficients, covariance matrix, $\hat\theta$ and its SE, log-likelihood,
number of iterations, a convergence flag, fitted values and the call.
Methods: `print`, `summary` (+ `print.summary`), `coef`, `vcov`, `logLik`
(with a `df` attribute, so `AIC()`/`BIC()` work), `fitted`, `residuals`
(response, Pearson; deviance for NB), `nobs` and `predict` with `newdata`
(`type = "response"`, `"count"`, `"zero"` and `"prob"` for ZINB). The
numerical work is in `R/utils.R` (weighted least squares, IRLS and
Newton–Raphson loops), `R/nbreg.R`, `R/zinbreg.R` and `R/zinb_hessian.R`;
none of it calls `optim()`, `glm()`, `lm()` or any other fitting routine.
Tests in `tests/testthat/` compare both functions with the reference
implementations and check offsets, weights, single-covariate models, EM
monotonicity, error messages and warnings. `devtools::check()` gives 0
errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes, and the GitHub Actions workflow runs it on
macOS, Windows and Linux.

A short example:

```{r usage, echo = TRUE}
fit <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + kid5 + ment | ment, data = bioChemists)
round(coef(fit), 3)
fit$theta
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(fem = "Women", kid5 = 0, ment = c(0, 20)),
        type = "zero")
```

# Benchmarking

```{r benchmark-fns}
nb_tol <- c(coefficients = 1e-5, std_errors = 1e-5, theta = 1e-4, loglik = 1e-4)
zinb_tol <- c(coefficients = 1e-3, std_errors = 1e-3, log_theta = 1e-3,
              loglik = 1e-3)

bench_nb <- function(f, data) {
  ours <- nbreg(f, data = data)
  ref <- glm.nb(f, data = data,
                control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-10, maxit = 100))
  tab <- data.frame(
    Term = c(names(coef(ours)), "theta"),
    nbreg = c(coef(ours), ours$theta),
    glm.nb = c(coef(ref), ref$theta),
    `SE nbreg` = c(sqrt(diag(vcov(ours))), ours$SE.theta),
    `SE glm.nb` = c(sqrt(diag(vcov(ref))), ref$SE.theta),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
  diffs <- c(coefficients = max(abs(coef(ours) - coef(ref))),
             std_errors = max(abs(sqrt(diag(vcov(ours))) - sqrt(diag(vcov(ref))))),
             theta = abs(ours$theta - ref$theta),
             loglik = abs(as.numeric(logLik(ours)) - as.numeric(logLik(ref))))
  time <- c(ours = system.time(nbreg(f, data = data))[["elapsed"]],
            ref = system.time(glm.nb(f, data = data,
                                     control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-10,
                                                           maxit = 100)))[["elapsed"]])
  list(tab = tab, diffs = diffs, time = time, ll = c(logLik(ours), logLik(ref)))
}

bench_zinb <- function(f, data) {
  ours <- zinbreg(f, data = data)
  ref <- zeroinfl(f, data = data, dist = "negbin",
                  control = zeroinfl.control(reltol = 1e-12))
  cf <- coef(ours)
  se_o <- sqrt(diag(vcov(ours)))
  se_r <- sqrt(diag(vcov(ref)))[names(cf)]
  tab <- data.frame(
    Term = c(names(cf), "Log(theta)"),
    zinbreg = c(cf, log(ours$theta)),
    zeroinfl = c(coef(ref)[names(cf)], log(ref$theta)),
    `SE zinbreg` = c(se_o, ours$SE.logtheta),
    `SE zeroinfl` = c(se_r, ref$SE.logtheta),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
  diffs <- c(coefficients = max(abs(cf - coef(ref)[names(cf)])),
             std_errors = max(abs(c(se_o - se_r, ours$SE.logtheta - ref$SE.logtheta))),
             log_theta = abs(log(ours$theta) - log(ref$theta)),
             loglik = abs(as.numeric(logLik(ours)) - as.numeric(logLik(ref))))
  time <- c(ours = system.time(zinbreg(f, data = data))[["elapsed"]],
            ref = system.time(zeroinfl(f, data = data, dist = "negbin",
                                       control = zeroinfl.control(reltol = 1e-12)))[["elapsed"]])
  list(tab = tab, diffs = diffs, time = time, ll = c(logLik(ours), logLik(ref)),
       iter = ours$iter)
}

f_bio_nb <- art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment
f_bio_zinb <- art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment
f_nmes_nb <- visits ~ hospital + health + chronic + gender + school + insurance
f_nmes_zinb <- visits ~ hospital + health + chronic + gender + school + insurance |
  hospital + chronic + gender + school + insurance

b_bio_nb <- bench_nb(f_bio_nb, bioChemists)
b_bio_zinb <- bench_zinb(f_bio_zinb, bioChemists)
b_nmes_nb <- bench_nb(f_nmes_nb, NMES1988)
b_nmes_zinb <- bench_zinb(f_nmes_zinb, NMES1988)
```

We compare our fits with `glm.nb()` (with `epsilon = 1e-10`) and
`zeroinfl()` (with `reltol = 1e-12`) on `pscl::bioChemists` (n = 915) and
`AER::NMES1988` (n = 4406), using the full models of Section 5 of the
project description. @tbl-agree summarizes the maximum absolute
differences. Every one is far inside the required tolerance. The
side-by-side estimates are in the appendix (@tbl-bio-nb to @tbl-nmes-zinb).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-agree
#| tbl-cap: "Maximum absolute difference from the reference implementation, with the required tolerance."
agree <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Coefficients", "Standard errors", "theta (NB) / log theta (ZINB)",
               "Log-likelihood"),
  `NB bioChemists` = b_bio_nb$diffs, `NB NMES1988` = b_nmes_nb$diffs,
  `NB tolerance` = nb_tol,
  `ZINB bioChemists` = b_bio_zinb$diffs, `ZINB NMES1988` = b_nmes_zinb$diffs,
  `ZINB tolerance` = zinb_tol,
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
agree[, -1] <- lapply(agree[, -1], function(v) formatC(v, format = "e", digits = 1))
kable(agree, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-time
#| tbl-cap: "Elapsed time (seconds) of one fit, and log-likelihoods."
timing <- data.frame(
  `Data / model` = c("bioChemists NB", "bioChemists ZINB", "NMES1988 NB",
                     "NMES1988 ZINB"),
  Ours = c(b_bio_nb$time[1], b_bio_zinb$time[1], b_nmes_nb$time[1],
           b_nmes_zinb$time[1]),
  Reference = c(b_bio_nb$time[2], b_bio_zinb$time[2], b_nmes_nb$time[2],
                b_nmes_zinb$time[2]),
  `logLik ours` = c(b_bio_nb$ll[1], b_bio_zinb$ll[1], b_nmes_nb$ll[1],
                    b_nmes_zinb$ll[1]),
  `logLik reference` = c(b_bio_nb$ll[2], b_bio_zinb$ll[2], b_nmes_nb$ll[2],
                         b_nmes_zinb$ll[2]),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(timing, digits = c(0, 3, 3, 4, 4))
```

`nbreg()` is about as fast as `glm.nb()`. `zinbreg()` is several times
slower than `zeroinfl()` because EM converges linearly: it needed
`r b_bio_zinb$iter` iterations on bioChemists and `r b_nmes_zinb$iter` on
NMES1988, each with a full IRLS fit in both M-steps. Every fit still takes
under a second.

```{r}
#| label: fig-em
#| fig-cap: "EM convergence of zinbreg() on NMES1988. Left: the observed-data log-likelihood at every iteration; the dashed line is the value from zeroinfl(). Right: the distance to the final log-likelihood, on a log scale."
#| fig-height: 3.2
m_em <- zinbreg(f_nmes_zinb, data = NMES1988)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(m_em, reference = b_nmes_zinb$ll[2])
plot(m_em, which = "gap")
```

@fig-em shows that the log-likelihood never decreases, as EM guarantees.
Almost all of the gain comes in the first few iterations. After that, the
distance to the optimum shrinks by a roughly constant factor per iteration,
a straight line on the log scale: the linear convergence typical of EM.

# Simulation study

```{r simulation}
#| cache: true
source(system.file("benchmark", "simulation.R", package = "nbzinbHossen"))
sim <- run_simulation(R = 200, n = 500, seed = 651)
```

We simulated $R = `r sim$R`$ data sets of size $n = `r sim$n`$ from a ZINB
model with $\log\mu_i = 1 + 0.5x_{1i} - 0.4x_{2i}$, where
$x_1\sim N(0,1)$ and $x_2\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5)$. The zero part is
$\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = -1 + 0.8w_i$ with $w\sim N(0,1)$, and
$\theta = 1.5$. Each data set was fitted with
`zinbreg(y ~ x1 + x2 | w)` (seed `r sim$seed`).
`r sim$n_ok` of `r sim$R` fits converged, with a median of
`r sim$median_iter` EM iterations. @tbl-sim reports the bias, the mean
estimated SE against the Monte Carlo SD of the estimates, and the coverage
of 95% Wald intervals. With 200 replications the Monte Carlo standard error
of a coverage near 0.95 is about 0.015.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sim
#| tbl-cap: "Simulation results (R = 200, n = 500)."
st <- sim$summary
names(st) <- c("Parameter", "True", "Mean estimate", "Bias", "MC SD",
               "Mean SE", "Coverage")
kable(st, digits = 3)
```

The estimates are close to unbiased. The largest bias, $-0.065$ for the
zero-part intercept, is less than a fifth of that estimate's Monte Carlo SD,
and the count-part slopes are essentially unbiased.

The average estimated SEs track the Monte Carlo SDs but are slightly smaller
for most parameters, most visibly for the binary covariate $x_2$ (0.121
against 0.141). Coverage of the 95% Wald intervals runs from 0.905 to 0.945.
With a Monte Carlo SE of about 0.015, the intervals for $x_2$ (0.905) and
$\log\theta$ (0.915) under-cover slightly.

Both shortfalls are plausible at $n = 500$. A binary covariate carries less
information than a continuous one, and $\theta$ is partly confounded with
the zero-inflation probability, since both change how many zeros appear. The
zero-part intercept is the least precisely estimated parameter (MC SD 0.36),
because only the zeros carry information about $\pi$.

# Data analysis: NMES1988

```{r nmes-fit}
d <- NMES1988
y <- d$visits
m_pois <- glm(f_nmes_nb, family = poisson, data = d)
m_nb <- nbreg(f_nmes_nb, data = d)
m_zinb <- zinbreg(f_nmes_zinb, data = d)
```

The data have $n = `r length(y)`$ individuals aged 66 and over. The response
is `visits`, the number of physician office visits. The count part uses
`hospital`, `health`, `chronic`, `gender`, `school` and `insurance`; the
zero part uses `hospital`, `chronic`, `gender`, `school` and `insurance`.

## Descriptive summary

```{r}
#| label: tbl-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Overdispersion and zeros in visits."
desc <- data.frame(n = length(y), Mean = mean(y), Variance = var(y),
                   `Variance / mean` = var(y) / mean(y),
                   `Observed zeros` = sum(y == 0),
                   `Proportion zero` = mean(y == 0),
                   `Poisson P(0) at mean` = dpois(0, mean(y)),
                   check.names = FALSE)
kable(desc, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-freq
#| fig-cap: "Observed frequencies of visits (bars, 30 = 30 or more) and frequencies expected under a Poisson distribution with the same mean (points)."
#| fig-height: 3.6
tab <- table(factor(pmin(y, 30), levels = 0:30))
bp <- barplot(tab, col = "grey80", border = "grey40",
              xlab = "Physician office visits", ylab = "Frequency",
              ylim = c(0, max(tab, length(y) * dpois(0:30, mean(y))) * 1.05))
points(bp, length(y) * dpois(0:30, mean(y)), pch = 19, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", c("Observed", "Poisson expected"), pch = c(22, 19),
       pt.bg = c("grey80", NA), pt.cex = c(2, 1),
       col = c("grey40", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

Visits are strongly overdispersed: the variance (45.7) is almost eight times
the mean (5.77). There are also far more zeros than a Poisson model allows.
683 people (15.5%) made no visits, while a Poisson distribution with the same
mean puts only 0.3% of its mass at zero, about 14 people. @fig-freq shows
the Poisson missing both the spike at zero and the long right tail, which
reaches 89 visits.

## Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison for NMES1988."
exp_zero <- c(Poisson = sum(dpois(0, fitted(m_pois))),
              NB = sum(dnbinom(0, size = m_nb$theta, mu = fitted(m_nb))),
              ZINB = sum(predict(m_zinb, type = "prob", at = 0)))
cmp <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Poisson (glm)", "NB (nbreg)", "ZINB (zinbreg)"),
  df = c(attr(logLik(m_pois), "df"), attr(logLik(m_nb), "df"),
         attr(logLik(m_zinb), "df")),
  logLik = c(logLik(m_pois), logLik(m_nb), logLik(m_zinb)),
  AIC = c(AIC(m_pois), AIC(m_nb), AIC(m_zinb)),
  BIC = c(BIC(m_pois), BIC(m_nb), BIC(m_zinb)),
  `Expected zeros` = exp_zero,
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kable(cmp, digits = 1)
```

The observed number of zeros is `r sum(y == 0)`. The NB model estimates
$\hat\theta = `r round(m_nb$theta, 3)`$ (SE `r round(m_nb$SE.theta, 3)`) and
the ZINB model $\hat\theta = `r round(m_zinb$theta, 3)`$
(SE `r round(m_zinb$SE.theta, 3)`).

The Poisson model fits very poorly: its AIC is about 11,600 higher than
NB's, and it predicts 47 zeros against 683. Allowing overdispersion closes
most of that gap. Unlike in the bioChemists example, though, the NB model
still under-predicts the zeros (608 against 683).

The ZINB model predicts 709 zeros, slightly too many but closer than NB.
Both criteria favour ZINB: its AIC is 148 lower and its BIC 109 lower, even
though BIC penalises its six extra parameters heavily. The log-likelihood
improves by 79.9.

A formal likelihood-ratio test is awkward because NB lies on the boundary of
the ZINB parameter space ($\pi \to 0$), but an improvement this large is far
beyond what six extra parameters produce by chance. The dispersion estimate
rises from 1.21 (NB) to 1.48 (ZINB), because the zero process now explains
part of the extra variation.

## Interpretation

```{r ci-helpers}
wald <- function(est, se) {
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", exp(est), exp(est - qnorm(0.975) * se),
          exp(est + qnorm(0.975) * se))
}
s_nb <- summary(m_nb)$coefficients[-1, ]
s_zc <- summary(m_zinb)$coefficients$count
s_zc <- s_zc[!(rownames(s_zc) %in% c("(Intercept)", "Log(theta)")), ]
s_zz <- summary(m_zinb)$coefficients$zero[-1, ]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-irr
#| tbl-cap: "Count part: incidence rate ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals."
kable(data.frame(Covariate = rownames(s_nb),
                 `NB IRR (95% CI)` = wald(s_nb[, 1], s_nb[, 2]),
                 `ZINB count IRR (95% CI)` = wald(s_zc[, 1], s_zc[, 2]),
                 `ZINB p-value` = format.pval(s_zc[, 4], digits = 2),
                 check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-or
#| tbl-cap: "ZINB zero part: odds ratios of being a structural zero (never visiting a physician), with 95% Wald confidence intervals."
kable(data.frame(Covariate = rownames(s_zz),
                 `OR (95% CI)` = wald(s_zz[, 1], s_zz[, 2]),
                 `p-value` = format.pval(s_zz[, 4], digits = 2),
                 check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lcc")
```

The number of doctor visits varies widely. The NB model allows more
variation than the Poisson model. At a mean of 5.77 visits, the estimated NB
variance is about 33.

In the ZINB count part, we compare people while keeping the other factors
the same:

- Each extra hospital stay is linked to 22% more expected visits.
- Poor health is linked to 33% more visits than average health.
- Excellent health is linked to 27% fewer visits than average health.
- Each extra chronic condition is linked to 14% more visits.
- Men have 8% fewer expected visits than women.
- Each extra year of schooling is linked to 2% more visits.
- Private insurance is linked to 13% more visits.

All these relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level.

The zero part describes the odds of being in the model's non-user group.
Each extra chronic condition lowers these odds by 71%. Private insurance
lowers them by 69%. Each extra year of schooling lowers them by 8%. Men have
almost twice the odds of women. Hospital stays are linked to lower odds, but
this result is not statistically significant.

Both models show similar patterns. Some differences are smaller in the ZINB
count part. For example, insurance is linked to 25% more visits in NB but
13% more in ZINB. ZINB also shows that insured people are less likely to
belong to the non-user group. People outside this group can still have zero
visits.

## Which model?

I prefer the ZINB model for these data. It has the lowest AIC and BIC of the
three, it reproduces the number of zeros better than NB, and its two parts
tell a sensible story about health-care use in old age. One process decides
whether a person sees a physician at all, and it depends strongly on chronic
illness, insurance, gender and education. A second process decides how
often users visit, and it depends mainly on health status and hospital
stays. The cost is six extra parameters and a slight over-prediction of
zeros (709 against 683). A hurdle model, which puts all zeros in one
process, would be a reasonable alternative to compare against.

# Discussion

The package reproduces `glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()` closely without a
general-purpose optimizer, but the approach has limits.

- **Speed.** EM converges only linearly (@fig-em): `zinbreg()` needed 66
  iterations on NMES1988 and 135 on bioChemists, and ran about 5 to 9 times
  slower than `zeroinfl()`. SQUAREM acceleration, or switching to Newton's
  method on the observed-data likelihood once EM is near the optimum, would
  cut this.
- **NB standard errors.** Like `glm.nb()`, `nbreg()` treats $\theta$ as known
  when computing $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$, so those SEs ignore the
  uncertainty in $\hat\theta$.
- **Interval coverage.** The simulation showed Wald intervals under-covering
  slightly at $n = 500$ (0.905 for the binary covariate). Profile-likelihood
  or bootstrap intervals would be more reliable.
- **Local maxima.** EM can in principle stop at a local maximum, so results
  depend on starting values. Ours (an NB fit plus a logistic regression of
  the zero indicator) reached the same optimum as `zeroinfl()` in every case
  tried, but that is not guaranteed.
- **Offsets.** Offsets are supported only in the count part.

Natural extensions are a zero-inflated Poisson option, hurdle models, robust
(sandwich) standard errors, a probit or complementary log-log link for the
zero part, and the Vuong test for comparing NB with ZINB.

# AI-use statement

I used Claude Code throughout this project, as the assignment intended.
Claude Code set up the package structure and CLAUDE.md, and wrote the
fitting code (IRLS for the NB coefficients, Newton–Raphson for $\log\theta$,
the EM algorithm and the analytic Hessian), the S3 methods, the tests, the
benchmark and simulation scripts, the GitHub Actions workflow and the
pkgdown configuration. It also drafted the other sections of this report
and all of its code. I wrote the interpretation of the NMES1988 results
(the Interpretation subsection) myself, rewrote the introduction in my own
words, and edited the other sections.

**What I verified myself:** I tested the package myself in R. I installed it
from GitHub with `devtools::install_github("armanhossen-am/nbzinbHossen")`,
and it installed without errors. I then ran the models myself, including the
`zinbreg()` example on the bioChemists data, and everything ran correctly:
the summary showed the count and zero-inflation coefficient tables, theta
and the log-likelihood, and `predict()` returned the structural-zero
probabilities.

**One improvement I directed:** I asked Claude Code to add a figure showing
the EM log-likelihood climbing at every iteration. I had it add this to the
package as a `plot()` method for `zinbreg` fits, with a test and
documentation, and commit both changes to GitHub.
